answer.diagnosis:
I found no clear shortcut in the weights. The trained layer-1 units fall into two families.

- **Small-blob detectors (units 2, 4, 14, 17, 18, 19, 25, 26, 29, 30):** centre-positive, ring-negative units with a positive bias and broadly positive periphery weights. They feed layer-2 units 9 and 11, which have negative output weights, so they push the logit toward 'small'.
- **Large-blob detectors (units 3, 7, 8, 21, 22, 24, 27, 28):** annulus-positive units with a negative centre, peaking at radius about 4-6 around the image centre. They feed layer-2 unit 1 and others with positive output weights, so they push the logit toward 'large'.
- **Untrained-looking units (the other 14):** weights of roughly ±25 with no spatial structure, consistent with random initialisation.

This readout depends on the radial extent of central brightness, i.e. blob size.

The one oddity is a scattered pixel pattern in the background. Examples are (1,0), (1,16-17), (3,12), (8,2), (19,2) and (20,19), plus (0,4), (0,11), (23,4) and (23,11). All units of one family share this pattern and the other family carries it with the opposite sign. It is not spatially coherent, though: there is no corner patch, border stripe, marker square or dedicated unit. That pattern fits all detectors of a family overfitting the same finite-sample background noise. A designed spurious cue would be expected to look localised.

The blob detectors are centred and roughly symmetric, so they show no position cue either. Since I found no localised feature that is correlated with the label and separate from size, I made no edits. A dataset-wide fixed texture cue cannot be ruled out from the weights alone, which is why confidence is 0.3 rather than near zero.
